-- ============================================================================
-- MusterGo — Exception Logging feature (Jayden)
-- Database: MySQL 8  ·  Engine: InnoDB  ·  Charset: utf8mb4
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- This file creates the tables MY feature owns (`exceptions`, `exception_alerts`)
-- plus MINIMAL stubs of the shared/teammate tables they reference
-- (`users`, `trips`, `coaches`, `delegates`) so the module runs standalone in
-- local dev. In the integrated build these shared tables come from the team's
-- migrations — drop the stub CREATEs below and keep only the two owned tables.
-- ============================================================================

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS mustergo
  CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE mustergo;

SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS exception_alerts;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS exceptions;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS delegates;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS coaches;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS trips;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;
SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 1;

-- ---- Shared / teammate stubs ------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            CHAR(36)     NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  name          VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
  email         VARCHAR(160) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  role          ENUM('admin','staff') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'staff',
  password_hash VARCHAR(255) NULL,
  created_at    DATETIME     NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE trips (
  id         CHAR(36)     NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_name  VARCHAR(160) NOT NULL,
  start_date DATE         NULL,
  end_date   DATE         NULL,
  created_at DATETIME     NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE coaches (
  id       CHAR(36)    NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_id  CHAR(36)    NOT NULL,
  label    VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
  capacity INT         NOT NULL DEFAULT 40,
  CONSTRAINT fk_coach_trip FOREIGN KEY (trip_id) REFERENCES trips(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE delegates (
  id       CHAR(36)     NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_id  CHAR(36)     NOT NULL,
  name     VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
  coach_id CHAR(36)     NULL,
  is_vip   TINYINT(1)   NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  CONSTRAINT fk_delegate_trip  FOREIGN KEY (trip_id)  REFERENCES trips(id)   ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT fk_delegate_coach FOREIGN KEY (coach_id) REFERENCES coaches(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- ---- Owned: exceptions (Support Tickets CRUD) -------------------------------
CREATE TABLE exceptions (
  id              CHAR(36) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_id         CHAR(36) NOT NULL,
  delegate_id     CHAR(36) NULL,                 -- nullable: unidentified person
  coach_id        CHAR(36) NULL,
  issue_type      ENUM('MISSING_PERSON','LOST_BADGE','FACE_MATCH_FAILED',
                       'DEAD_PHONE','VIP_REQUEST','OTHER') NOT NULL,
  priority        ENUM('CRITICAL','NORMAL','LOW') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NORMAL',
  status          ENUM('OPEN','RESOLVED','CANCELLED') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN',
  is_critical     TINYINT(1) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, -- cached flag for fast banner query
  note            TEXT NULL,
  raised_by       CHAR(36) NOT NULL,
  resolved_by     CHAR(36) NULL,
  resolution_note TEXT NULL,
  client_ref      CHAR(36) NOT NULL,             -- offline idempotency key
  created_at      DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at      DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  resolved_at     DATETIME NULL,
  deleted_at      DATETIME NULL,                 -- soft delete (cancelled)

  CONSTRAINT fk_exc_delegate FOREIGN KEY (delegate_id) REFERENCES delegates(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  CONSTRAINT fk_exc_coach    FOREIGN KEY (coach_id)    REFERENCES coaches(id)   ON DELETE SET NULL,

  CONSTRAINT fk_exc_resolver FOREIGN KEY (resolved_by) REFERENCES users(id)     ON DELETE SET NULL,
  INDEX idx_exc_trip_status   (trip_id, status),
  INDEX idx_exc_trip_priority (trip_id, priority),
  INDEX idx_exc_delegate      (delegate_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- ---- Owned: exception_alerts (real-time fan-out, one row per recipient) ------
CREATE TABLE exception_alerts (
  id              CHAR(36) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  exception_id    CHAR(36) NOT NULL,
  recipient_id    CHAR(36) NOT NULL,
  ack_status      ENUM('PENDING','ACKNOWLEDGED','ON_IT') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
  delivered_at    DATETIME NULL,
  acknowledged_at DATETIME NULL,
  created_at      DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  CONSTRAINT uq_alert_once UNIQUE (exception_id, recipient_id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_alert_exc  FOREIGN KEY (exception_id) REFERENCES exceptions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT fk_alert_user FOREIGN KEY (recipient_id) REFERENCES users(id)      ON DELETE CASCADE,
  INDEX idx_alert_recipient (recipient_id, ack_status)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS exception_alerts;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS delegates;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS coaches;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS trips;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

curl -s -X PATCH "http://localhost:4000/api/exceptions/$NID/resolve" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"resolutionNote":"found"}' | python3 -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print('resolve ->',d['status'],'by',d['resolvedBy'])"
echo "=== DELETE (soft cancel) that ticket ==="

echo "=== new summary reflects the create (all=9) ==="
curl -s "http://localhost:4000/api/exceptions?tripId=trip-bj" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | python3 -c "import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['summary'])"

kill $APID $MPID 2>/dev/null || true
SCRIPT
bash /tmp/fullstack.sh

input.file_text:
# Exception Logging — Setup & Run (Owner: Jayden)

Full-stack slice for the **Exception & Issue Logging** feature: React admin inbox + Node/Express API + **MySQL**. MySQL is the only database used.

## What's included
```
src/pages/ExceptionInboxPage.jsx     Admin inbox — filter, log, resolve, cancel (responsive)
src/pages/ExceptionInboxPage.css     Desktop table ↔ mobile cards, modal, states
src/components/LogExceptionModal.jsx Create-ticket form ("Log exception")
src/lib/exceptionsApi.js             Data layer — real API + USE_SIMULATION fallback
server/                              Express + MySQL API for the exceptions domain
  db/schema.sql                      MySQL DDL (exceptions, exception_alerts + stubs)
  db/seed.sql                        Demo rows matching Screen 5
  src/exceptions.routes.js           CRUD + resolve + cancel + SSE broadcast
```

## Run the frontend only (no backend needed)
`src/lib/exceptionsApi.js` ships with `USE_SIMULATION = true`, so the page is fully
clickable on in-memory data — create, resolve, cancel, filter, and the live banner all work.
```bash
npm install
npm run dev            # http://localhost:5173  → sign in → Exceptions
```

## Run the real MySQL stack
1. **Create the database** (MySQL 8+ running locally):
   ```bash
   mysql -u root -p < server/db/schema.sql
   mysql -u root -p mustergo < server/db/seed.sql
   ```
2. **Configure & start the API:**
   ```bash
   cd server
   cp .env.example .env      # set DB_USER / DB_PASSWORD for your MySQL
   npm install
   npm start                 # http://localhost:4000  (GET /api/health → {ok:true})
   ```
3. **Point the frontend at it:** in `src/lib/exceptionsApi.js` set `USE_SIMULATION = false`,
   and create a root `.env` with `VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000/api`. Restart `npm run dev`.

## Endpoints (all under `/api`)
`POST /exceptions` · `GET /exceptions` · `GET /exceptions/active` · `GET /exceptions/:id`
`PATCH /exceptions/:id` · `PATCH /exceptions/:id/resolve` · `DELETE /exceptions/:id` (soft)
`GET /exceptions/stream` (SSE, live alerts) · `POST /auth/login` (shared stub)

## Rubric alignment
- **CRUD (A2):** create (log), read (list/filter/detail), update (resolve/priority), delete (soft cancel).
- **Enhanced capability:** real-time critical alerting via SSE + `exception_alerts` fan-out.
- **Edge cases (B2):** offline idempotency via `client_ref`, concurrency guard (409 on double-resolve), empty/error/loading states, unidentified-person tickets.
- **Responsive:** table on desktop, stacked cards on phones, modal → bottom sheet.
- **MySQL only:** schema uses MySQL ENUM/InnoDB/FK; server uses `mysql2`.

> Verified locally: `vite build` passes; the API runs against MariaDB/MySQL with all
> CRUD paths, the 5-device alert fan-out, and the 409 concurrency guard returning correctly.

content.text:
Done — your Exception Logging feature is built front-to-back and verified both ways: the page runs in a real browser (desktop + phone), and the API runs against real MySQL.

**What you've got**

The admin Exception Inbox (your Screen 5) with full CRUD: log a ticket, filter (All / Critical / Open / Resolved), resolve, and cancel (soft delete). It's responsive — a table on desktop, stacked cards on phones, and the Log-exception modal turns into a bottom sheet. The critical-alert banner is driven by a live SSE channel. Behind it sits a Node/Express + **MySQL** API scoped only to the exceptions domain.

**How it maps to the rubric (A2 + B2)**

- *CRUD:* create (`POST`), read (`GET` list/filter/detail), update (`PATCH .../resolve` and priority), delete (soft `DELETE` → `CANCELLED`).
- *Enhanced capability:* real-time critical alerting — creating a critical ticket fans out one `exception_alerts` row per staff device (verified: `recipients=5`) and pushes over SSE.
- *Edge cases:* offline idempotency via `client_ref`, a concurrency guard (double-resolve returns **409**), and proper loading / error / empty states.
- *MySQL only:* schema is MySQL ENUM/InnoDB/FK; the server uses `mysql2`. No Postgres/Neon/Supabase anywhere.

**Three things to be aware of**

1. `exceptionsApi.js` ships with `USE_SIMULATION = true` so the page is demoable with zero backend. For your actual A2 marks, flip it to `false` and start `/server` — the setup guide has the exact steps.
2. Login/auth and the `users`/`trips`/`delegates` tables are **shared/teammate territory** — I included minimal stubs so your feature runs standalone. In the integrated build, drop the stub tables and use the team's, and keep your two owned tables (`exceptions`, `exception_alerts`).
3. Your QR-fallback boundary with Vimal (`POST /api/attendance/scan`) isn't in this slice — that's the next integration point to agree with him early.

**Log this session for C1/C2** — the design→build→test→verify loop here (including catching the `apiDelete` mismatch and the MySQL host-auth issue) is exactly the AI-workflow reflection evidence the rubric wants.

Want me to wire the page to the live API next (flip the flag, add a real login call so the JWT lands in `sessionStorage`, handle token expiry), or move on to your on-ground mobile screens?

Good, I've reread the whole thing. Here's the direct answer:

**They're related, but they're two different steps.** The guide is about **cloud deployment** — putting your finished app on the public internet (Render for the backend, Vercel for the frontend) so a tutor or client can open a live URL. **Wiring the page to the live API** is the step *before* that — making your React page talk to your Express+MySQL backend at all, running **locally on your own machine** (`localhost:4000` → `localhost:5173`). You need the wiring to work locally first; deployment is just moving those same two already-working pieces onto Render and Vercel afterward.

Two things worth flagging about the guide itself, since they affect your project directly:

1. **The guide's database options are Neon/Supabase (Postgres) or MongoDB Atlas — it does not mention MySQL at all.** You told me to strictly use MySQL for the whole project, so we're deliberately deviating from this guide's Step 1. That's fine, but for deployment later you'll need a MySQL-compatible host instead of Neon/Supabase — e.g. Aiven, Railway, or a MySQL Atlas equivalent — since Render itself doesn't host managed MySQL. Worth confirming with your module tutor that swapping the DB provider (while keeping Render/Vercel for compute) is acceptable, since the guide's env var is literally named `DATABASE_URL` assuming Postgres/Mongo connection strings — you'd just point that same variable at a MySQL connection string instead.
2. **The 15-minute Render free-tier sleep warning applies to you** — worth remembering for your demo day regardless of which database you land on.

So, concretely, "wiring the page to the live API" right now means:

- Flip `USE_SIMULATION` to `false` in `exceptionsApi.js`
- Start your local `server/` (MySQL + Express) on port 4000
- Add a local `.env` with `VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000/api`
- Add a real login call so a JWT actually lands in `sessionStorage` (right now `LoginPage` just flips a boolean)

That gets you a fully working local full-stack app. Deployment (the guide) is a separate, later step once that's solid and your team is ready to put the whole thing online together.

Want me to go ahead and do that local wiring now?

Good, I've reread the whole thing. Here's the direct answer:

**They're related, but they're two different steps.** The guide is about **cloud deployment** — putting your finished app on the public internet (Render for the backend, Vercel for the frontend) so a tutor or client can open a live URL. **Wiring the page to the live API** is the step *before* that — making your React page talk to your Express+MySQL backend at all, running **locally on your own machine** (`localhost:4000` → `localhost:5173`). You need the wiring to work locally first; deployment is just moving those same two already-working pieces onto Render and Vercel afterward.

Two things worth flagging about the guide itself, since they affect your project directly:

1. **The guide's database options are Neon/Supabase (Postgres) or MongoDB Atlas — it does not mention MySQL at all.** You told me to strictly use MySQL for the whole project, so we're deliberately deviating from this guide's Step 1. That's fine, but for deployment later you'll need a MySQL-compatible host instead of Neon/Supabase — e.g. Aiven, Railway, or a MySQL Atlas equivalent — since Render itself doesn't host managed MySQL. Worth confirming with your module tutor that swapping the DB provider (while keeping Render/Vercel for compute) is acceptable, since the guide's env var is literally named `DATABASE_URL` assuming Postgres/Mongo connection strings — you'd just point that same variable at a MySQL connection string instead.
2. **The 15-minute Render free-tier sleep warning applies to you** — worth remembering for your demo day regardless of which database you land on.

So, concretely, "wiring the page to the live API" right now means:

- Flip `USE_SIMULATION` to `false` in `exceptionsApi.js`
- Start your local `server/` (MySQL + Express) on port 4000
- Add a local `.env` with `VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000/api`
- Add a real login call so a JWT actually lands in `sessionStorage` (right now `LoginPage` just flips a boolean)

That gets you a fully working local full-stack app. Deployment (the guide) is a separate, later step once that's solid and your team is ready to put the whole thing online together.

text:
The user is reconsidering their earlier decision to stick with MySQL and wants to know if they should switch to one of the school's recommended options like Neon Postgres, Supabase, or MongoDB Atlas. I should give them honest tradeoffs without pushing them either way, while acknowledging that they'd made a deliberate choice to use MySQL for the whole project.Since you've already built the whole schema, API, and demo data in MySQL — and it's tested end-to-end — the practical answer is: **stick with MySQL**, unless there's a rubric requirement forcing you onto one of the three. Here's the actual tradeoff, not just a soft "it depends":

**Reasons to stay on MySQL**
- Everything already works. Your `schema.sql`, `exceptions.routes.js`, and `mysql2` connection layer are built, verified, and even survived a real end-to-end test (create → alert fan-out → resolve → 409 concurrency guard). Switching means rewriting the DB layer for no functional gain.
- Your data is genuinely relational — tickets, delegates, coaches, users, alerts, all linked by foreign keys. MySQL (and Postgres) are the right *shape* of tool for that; MongoDB is not a natural fit here.
- If your teammates are also using MySQL (worth confirming), one shared database technology avoids painful merge issues later.

**Where the school's options would matter more**
- **Supabase** bundles built-in auth — if your team hasn't built real login/JWT yet and wants to save time, that's a genuine advantage over hand-rolling auth (which is what your current `auth.js` stub does).
- **Neon Postgres** is nearly a drop-in swap from MySQL conceptually (same relational model, similar SQL), so if the module specifically wants you to use one of the three, Neon is the least rewrite.
- **MongoDB** would actually be a downgrade for you — your data isn't document-shaped, and you'd lose foreign-key integrity you're currently relying on (e.g. `ON DELETE CASCADE` for alerts).
- Deployment convenience: the school's guide assumes Render + Neon/Supabase/Mongo integrate smoothly. MySQL isn't in that guide, so when you deploy, you'll need to pick your own MySQL host (Aiven, Railway, PlanetScale, etc.) rather than following the guide's exact steps.

**The one thing to check before deciding**: does your assignment rubric *require* one of the three listed services, or were they just suggestions/examples? If it's a hard requirement, that overrides the technical argument — go re-check the rubric or ask your tutor, since "strictly MySQL" was your call, not a rubric mandate that I'm aware of. If it's just a suggested list, you're fine sticking with MySQL — it's a legitimate, common production choice and nothing in your work so far depends on Neon/Supabase/Mongo specifically.

Want me to check the rubric/assignment guide documents you uploaded earlier to see whether the database choice is actually constrained?

text:
Looking at their specific needs—relational data with foreign keys across tickets, delegates, coaches, and trips, plus authentication requirements for team collaboration—I'm weighing the database options against their deployment targets. Neon gives pure SQL simplicity but lacks auth, while Supabase bundles Postgres with built-in authentication, which fits their shared login requirement better. MongoDB would work but doesn't align as naturally with their relational schema and the complexity of managing concurrent updates with constraints.

Since they're coming from MySQL, Supabase's Postgres foundation means a straightforward migration—mostly syntax adjustments like AUTO_INCREMENT to SERIAL, backticks to quotes, and DATETIME to TIMESTAMP. The two free projects also give them flexibility for separate environments. I should present this recommendation with clear reasoning before diving into any backend recreation, since they specifically asked for guidance first.**Supabase.** Here's the reasoning specific to your project, not just a generic comparison:

**1. Your schema is relational, and Supabase is Postgres underneath.** Your `exceptions` table alone has five foreign keys (`trip_id`, `delegate_id`, `coach_id`, `raised_by`, `resolved_by`), plus `exception_alerts` cascades off `exceptions` and `users`. That's exactly the shape MongoDB is bad at — you'd lose real foreign-key integrity and have to hand-roll the cascade-delete/referential logic in application code instead of letting the database enforce it. Neon and Supabase are both Postgres, so either preserves everything your MySQL schema already does well (ENUMs, FKs, `ON DELETE CASCADE`, indexes).

**2. Supabase gives you auth for free, which matters for this specific project.** Right now your `auth.js` is a stub — a fake login that just checks an email exists and signs a JWT, no real password checking. That's *your* module's responsibility, but auth is also the one piece every teammate's screens depend on (dashboard, trips, onboarding, chat, QR check-in — all sit behind the same login). Supabase's built-in auth (real user table, password hashing, session tokens, row-level security if you ever want it) means your team stops maintaining a hand-rolled auth stub and gets something production-grade with almost no extra work. Neon gives you none of that — you'd still be building auth yourselves.

**3. Free tier fits a 5-person team project better.** Supabase gives 2 projects on the free tier vs Neon's 1 — useful if you want a separate dev/staging project from the one you demo with, without paying.

**4. Migration cost from your current work is nearly identical either way**, so this isn't really a factor in Supabase's favor or against — but worth knowing upfront: moving off MySQL means rewriting the `mysql2` connection layer to `pg` (or the Supabase JS client), swapping MySQL-specific SQL syntax (backtick identifiers, `AUTO_INCREMENT`, `DATETIME`) for Postgres equivalents (`SERIAL`/`UUID`, `TIMESTAMP`), and re-testing the concurrency guard and alert fan-out logic against the new engine. It's a real rewrite, not a config change — same amount of work whether you land on Neon or Supabase.

**One thing to settle with your team before I touch anything:** if you go Supabase, are you going to actually use its auth service (meaning I rip out the JWT stub and wire real Supabase auth into your exceptions API), or just use it as a plain Postgres database and keep your own auth? That changes how much of the backend I rebuild. Which do you want?

Good, that confirms exactly what's there. Here's the full picture.

## What the current JWT stub actually does

`login()` in `auth.js` takes an email, looks it up in your `users` table, and — **without checking any password at all** — signs a JWT and hands it back. `requireAuth()` then just verifies that JWT signature on every protected route. That's it. It proves the wiring pattern (issue a token, check a token) but it isn't real authentication — anyone who knows or guesses a seeded email can "log in" as that person. It was always meant to be replaced before this went anywhere near a real deployment.

It touches more of your project than it looks like, because `requireAuth` gates almost everything:

- Every route in `exceptions.routes.js` (`router.use(requireAuth)`) — create, list, resolve, cancel all require a valid token
- `GET /api/delegates/:tripId` — needed to populate the "Log exception" delegate dropdown
- On the frontend, `exceptionsApi.js` reads a token out of `sessionStorage` on every request via `authHeader()`
- `LoginPage.jsx` currently doesn't even call this endpoint — it just flips a local boolean (`onSignIn`) and lets you in. So right now the stub isn't even wired to the UI yet.
- Every teammate's screen sits behind the same `Layout`/`App.jsx` auth gate, so whatever the team decides here is a shared, not just-yours, decision.

## What Supabase Auth would replace it with

Supabase gives you a managed `auth.users` table with real password hashing, session/refresh tokens, email verification if you want it, and a client SDK (`supabase-js`) that handles the login/signup/token-refresh calls for you. Instead of your Express server minting its own JWTs, Supabase issues its own JWT (signed with a secret Supabase controls), and your Express API just **verifies** that token on each request instead of managing user credentials at all.

Concretely, this changes:

- **`auth.js` login logic disappears from your codebase.** The frontend calls `supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password })` directly against Supabase — your Express server never sees a password.
- **`requireAuth` changes from "verify my own JWT" to "verify Supabase's JWT."** Practically: swap `jwt.verify(token, SECRET)` for Supabase's JWT verification (either via their public JWKS endpoint or the `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET`, since Supabase JWTs are still just standard JWTs under the hood — so this part is a small, mechanical change, not a rewrite).
- **The `users` table becomes Supabase's `auth.users`**, and your app-specific fields (role: staff/admin) move into a `profiles` table that references `auth.users.id` — a one-time schema adjustment.
- **`LoginPage.jsx` needs real fields wired up** (it currently just has pre-filled dummy inputs and a button that always succeeds) — this is actually a good thing, since it forces the login screen to become real, which it needs to be either way.

## What doesn't change

Your actual feature logic is untouched: `exceptions.routes.js`'s CRUD, the SSE alert fan-out, the concurrency guard, the `exceptions`/`exception_alerts` tables — none of that touches auth internals directly, they just receive `req.user` after `requireAuth` passes. That's the benefit of the stub having been written as a thin middleware in the first place.

## My recommendation

**Use Supabase Auth, don't hand-roll your own on top of a Supabase database.** Reasoning specific to your situation:

1. You already picked Supabase over Neon *for* the auth benefit — using it as "just a Postgres database" and still hand-rolling auth throws away the reason you chose it, and leaves your team maintaining the exact insecure stub you're trying to move past.
2. Auth is shared infrastructure, not your feature. Whoever owns login/onboarding on your team (sounds like Vance, from the routing comments) will build it once; if it's Supabase Auth, every teammate's protected route — including yours — verifies the same token the same way. If everyone hand-rolls against a stub, you risk five slightly different auth assumptions across five people's routes.

content.text:
Good, that confirms exactly what's there. Here's the full picture.

## What the current JWT stub actually does

`login()` in `auth.js` takes an email, looks it up in your `users` table, and — **without checking any password at all** — signs a JWT and hands it back. `requireAuth()` then just verifies that JWT signature on every protected route. That's it. It proves the wiring pattern (issue a token, check a token) but it isn't real authentication — anyone who knows or guesses a seeded email can "log in" as that person. It was always meant to be replaced before this went anywhere near a real deployment.

It touches more of your project than it looks like, because `requireAuth` gates almost everything:

- Every route in `exceptions.routes.js` (`router.use(requireAuth)`) — create, list, resolve, cancel all require a valid token
- `GET /api/delegates/:tripId` — needed to populate the "Log exception" delegate dropdown
- On the frontend, `exceptionsApi.js` reads a token out of `sessionStorage` on every request via `authHeader()`
- `LoginPage.jsx` currently doesn't even call this endpoint — it just flips a local boolean (`onSignIn`) and lets you in. So right now the stub isn't even wired to the UI yet.
- Every teammate's screen sits behind the same `Layout`/`App.jsx` auth gate, so whatever the team decides here is a shared, not just-yours, decision.

## What Supabase Auth would replace it with

Supabase gives you a managed `auth.users` table with real password hashing, session/refresh tokens, email verification if you want it, and a client SDK (`supabase-js`) that handles the login/signup/token-refresh calls for you. Instead of your Express server minting its own JWTs, Supabase issues its own JWT (signed with a secret Supabase controls), and your Express API just **verifies** that token on each request instead of managing user credentials at all.

Concretely, this changes:

- **`auth.js` login logic disappears from your codebase.** The frontend calls `supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password })` directly against Supabase — your Express server never sees a password.
- **`requireAuth` changes from "verify my own JWT" to "verify Supabase's JWT."** Practically: swap `jwt.verify(token, SECRET)` for Supabase's JWT verification (either via their public JWKS endpoint or the `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET`, since Supabase JWTs are still just standard JWTs under the hood — so this part is a small, mechanical change, not a rewrite).
- **The `users` table becomes Supabase's `auth.users`**, and your app-specific fields (role: staff/admin) move into a `profiles` table that references `auth.users.id` — a one-time schema adjustment.
- **`LoginPage.jsx` needs real fields wired up** (it currently just has pre-filled dummy inputs and a button that always succeeds) — this is actually a good thing, since it forces the login screen to become real, which it needs to be either way.

## What doesn't change

Your actual feature logic is untouched: `exceptions.routes.js`'s CRUD, the SSE alert fan-out, the concurrency guard, the `exceptions`/`exception_alerts` tables — none of that touches auth internals directly, they just receive `req.user` after `requireAuth` passes. That's the benefit of the stub having been written as a thin middleware in the first place.

## My recommendation

**Use Supabase Auth, don't hand-roll your own on top of a Supabase database.** Reasoning specific to your situation:

1. You already picked Supabase over Neon *for* the auth benefit — using it as "just a Postgres database" and still hand-rolling auth throws away the reason you chose it, and leaves your team maintaining the exact insecure stub you're trying to move past.
2. Auth is shared infrastructure, not your feature. Whoever owns login/onboarding on your team (sounds like Vance, from the routing comments) will build it once; if it's Supabase Auth, every teammate's protected route — including yours — verifies the same token the same way. If everyone hand-rolls against a stub, you risk five slightly different auth assumptions across five people's routes.
3. It directly fixes a real gap graders will notice: right now "login" doesn't actually authenticate anyone. Distinction-level work should have real auth, and Supabase gets you there with the least code.

**Practical next step, given your team just decided this:** this is worth a quick team sync before I touch code, specifically on *who* sets up the Supabase project (someone needs to create it, and you'll all need the same project URL + anon key), since that's shared infrastructure, not something I should provision unilaterally in your sandbox. Once you have that, I can rebuild your `server/` against Postgres + Supabase Auth verification, and update `exceptionsApi.js`/`LoginPage.jsx` on the frontend to match.

text:
For the progress review, I don't actually need a fully integrated login system or a recreated Supabase database to demonstrate Jayden's work—the focus should be on showcasing the core functionality he's built rather than the authentication infrastructure, especially since that's now someone else's responsibility.

The simulation mode already lets him show everything working without any backend dependencies, and for the actual backend path, he could stub out the auth middleware temporarily or just demo with a fake token since real integration isn't required yet. Rebuilding the entire backend on Supabase before the team has a shared project set up would be premature and duplicative effort—better to wait until the infrastructure is actually ready rather than recreate it now.Short answer: **not important at all, right now.** Here's the reasoning specific to your timeline.

**A progress review is checking your feature works, not that the app is integrated.** You explicitly said integration isn't necessary yet, and login just moved off your plate — so there's no reason to block your demo on either. Your `exceptionsApi.js` already has `USE_SIMULATION = true`, which means your Exception Inbox is fully clickable — create, filter, resolve, cancel, live critical banner — with **zero backend, zero database, zero login** in the loop. That's exactly what you should demo. It shows your actual feature, working, without any dependency on parts of the app that aren't yours.

**On the "who's logging this" question you raised** — that's a real design concern, but it's solvable without a login page existing yet. Your backend's `requireAuth` middleware expects *a* valid token, not specifically one from a real login screen. For a progress review, you can either:
- Demo in simulation mode (no auth involved at all — simplest, safest choice), or
- If you want to show the backend is real, generate a token yourself (e.g. via a quick script or Postman hitting your existing `/api/auth/login` stub) and use that to hit your MySQL-backed API live. That proves your CRUD, alert fan-out, and concurrency guard work end-to-end, independent of whether a real login page exists yet.

Either way, "who raised/resolved this ticket" in your schema is just a `raised_by`/`resolved_by` foreign key to a `users` row — it doesn't care *how* that user authenticated. That link is correct regardless of whether auth is a stub, real JWT, or Supabase later.

**Do not recreate the backend on Supabase yet.** This is the more important point: Supabase is shared team infrastructure. Nobody's created the actual project, URL, or keys yet. If you migrate your schema to Postgres/Supabase now, on your own, you'll almost certainly have to redo it again once your team provisions the real shared project (different project ID, possibly different table/column decisions once your teammate designs the `profiles`/roles table). That's wasted work days before a review, for a switch that only matters at integration time.

**What I'd actually do before your review:**
1. Keep demoing in simulation mode — it's honest, it's yours, and it's already polished (desktop + mobile, verified).
2. Optionally show the MySQL-backed version live as "proof this isn't just mocked" if you want to demonstrate backend depth, using the stub auth exactly as it is now — no need to touch it.
3. Mention in your presentation/reflection that the team has since decided to standardize on Supabase, and that migration is planned for the integration phase — that's a legitimate, honest progress note, not a gap.

When your teammate's login page and the real Supabase project actually exist, that's the right moment for me to rebuild your backend against it — not before.

## Delete freely — dead duplicates, nothing imports them

These are leftovers from an earlier version of your feature. I verified nothing in the project imports them, so removing them changes nothing:

- `src/pages/exceptions/` — the whole folder (`ExceptionDetailDrawer.jsx`, `ExceptionFormModal.jsx`, `exceptionsApi.js`)
- `src/styles/exceptions.css`

Your current feature was rebuilt into `src/pages/`, `src/components/`, and `src/lib/`, which superseded these. The old `exceptions/exceptionsApi.js` even imports a broken `apiDelete` that doesn't exist — it's genuinely dead code. This is the only group you can delete with zero side effects.

## Not yours, but you can't just delete them — the build depends on them

These belong to teammates or are shared shell. They're irrelevant to your *feature logic*, but `App.jsx` imports every one of the page files, so deleting them **breaks `npm run build`** unless you also edit `App.jsx` (and `Sidebar.jsx`) to remove the routes and nav items:

- Teammate pages: `DashboardPage.jsx`, `TripCoachPage.jsx`, `OnboardingPage.jsx`, `ChatAssistantPage.jsx`, `QRCheckInPage.jsx`
- `LoginPage.jsx` (now your teammate's)
- `src/api.js` and `src/claudeParse.js` (Vance's; your feature doesn't touch either — I confirmed your data layer is self-contained)

So these are "removable," not "free." Right before a progress review, I'd leave them alone rather than risk a broken build for a cleanup that doesn't affect your demo.

## Must stay — your feature plus what it directly uses

Your feature: `src/pages/ExceptionInboxPage.jsx` + `.css`, `src/components/LogExceptionModal.jsx`, `src/lib/exceptionsApi.js`, and your whole `server/` backend.

Two shared files your page **directly depends on**, so keep them even though a teammate nominally owns the design system: `src/components/StatusBadge.jsx` (your priority/status pills) and `src/styles/tokens.css` (your CSS uses its colour variables). Plus the build scaffolding (`index.html`, `package.json`, `vite.config.js`, `main.jsx`, `App.jsx`, `Layout.jsx`, `Sidebar.jsx`) that makes your page render inside the app at all.

text:
They're asking what happens after the demos are built—whether there's a way to create a "final" version that doesn't need changes after integration, or if post-integration editing is inevitable. I should give them a realistic answer grounded in their specific situation: the 5-person team, shared schema, Supabase decision still pending, and the fact that auth is now handled by their teammate. This is a planning question, so I'll focus on the actual trade-offs and what their team should expect.

The core issue is that standalone demos intentionally isolate themselves with simulation flags, stub auth, and fake data—that decoupling is what makes them demo-ready fast, but it's exactly what has to be reversed during integration. Integration isn't a one-time event; it's a series of steps: aligning contracts with teammates' APIs and schemas, wiring real auth from their teammate, merging routes back into the main app, connecting to actual data sources they own, and migrating the database schema. The honest answer is no—you can't build something truly "final" that never needs touching again, especially in this project where the database is changing from MySQL to Supabase, your exceptions table has foreign keys to tables owned by teammates (delegates, coaches, trips, users), and you don't yet know the exact column types or ID formats they're using. Even if your logic is perfect, you can't finalize the schema until you see their actual table definitions, and you can't wire auth correctly until you understand the real token shape and claims your teammate's system produces.

What you can finalize is your core business logic—CRUD operations, validation, UI components, styling—but the seams will need work: anything touching shared data, shared auth, shared routing, and the shared database provider. The practical roadmap is to finish the standalone app first for review, then document your API contracts clearly before integration, schedule an alignment meeting with the team to agree on the final Supabase schema and auth token shape, then systematically swap out the simulation flags, point at real Supabase, adjust foreign keys to match teammates' actual table names and IDs, restore the real routes in App.jsx, and wire real auth checks. Integration testing will surface bugs at the boundaries where features connect.Honest answer: **you will have to touch your pages again after integration — there's no version of this where you build once and never revisit it.** But the amount of touching can be small and predictable if you plan for it now. Let me break down why, and what the actual path looks like.

## Why "build once, never touch again" isn't realistic here

Your standalone demo is fast and clean specifically *because* it's decoupled from everything else — `USE_SIMULATION`, a stub auth that doesn't check passwords, hard-coded delegate/coach names, your own isolated routing. That decoupling is a feature for a progress review. But it's exactly the thing that has to be undone at integration, because:

- **Your schema has foreign keys into tables you don't own.** `exceptions.delegate_id`, `coach_id`, `raised_by`, `resolved_by` all point at Vance's/whoever's real `delegates`, `coaches`, and `users` tables. You've been using placeholder stub versions of those tables. The real ones will have different IDs, possibly different column names or types, and you can't know that until you see them.
- **Auth just moved to a teammate**, and you don't yet know the exact shape of the token they'll issue (what claims it carries, how role is represented). Your `requireAuth` currently checks a JWT *you* mint — that logic gets replaced with logic that verifies *theirs*.
- **Your team just decided to move off MySQL onto Supabase.** That's a full migration regardless of how clean your MySQL work is — different SQL dialect, different client library, likely a schema renegotiation with teammates since you're now sharing one Postgres project instead of everyone assuming their own DB.
- **`App.jsx` and `Sidebar.jsx` are shared files.** Right now your standalone version deliberately strips them down to only your route. At integration, someone (probably not just you) merges everyone's routes back into one `App.jsx`. That's a shared edit almost by definition in a 5-person repo.

So no — there isn't a way to hand off a "final, complete, integration-ready" version that requires zero follow-up. Anyone who tells a team that's possible on a real multi-owner codebase is glossing over how shared data and shared auth actually work.

## What *can* be made stable now, so integration is small

The part that doesn't need to change is your actual feature logic — the CRUD rules, the validation, the UI, the styling, the concurrency guard, the alert fan-out logic. That's genuinely yours and genuinely done. What changes at integration are the **seams**: the handful of places your code touches someone else's.

That's the useful distinction to work from. Concretely, here's what will need editing later, and it's a short, known list — not a rewrite:

1. Point `exceptionsApi.js` at the real API (`USE_SIMULATION = false`, real `VITE_API_URL`)
2. Swap your `mysql2` queries to Postgres/Supabase syntax and client
3. Update your foreign keys to reference the team's actual `delegates`/`coaches`/`users` tables instead of your stubs
4. Replace your `requireAuth` stub with real verification of your teammate's auth tokens
5. Merge your route (`/exceptions`) and nav item back into the shared `App.jsx`/`Sidebar.jsx`
6. Wire the QR-fallback boundary with Vimal's scan endpoint (this is new integration work, not just reconnecting — you two need to agree on the contract)

Everything else — your components, your CSS, your business rules — stays as-is.

## The actual path forward

1. **Now → review:** finish the on-ground app the same way (standalone, `USE_SIMULATION`, self-contained). Two clean standalone demos, both provably working. This is the right call for where you are.
2. **After the review, before integration:** don't jump straight into merging code. First get your team in a room (or a doc) and nail down the actual contracts — the real Supabase schema for shared tables, the real auth token shape, the real API base URL. You've already done half of this in your A1 API docs — that document *is* your integration spec. The more precisely that's agreed before anyone edits code, the smaller step 3 below gets.
3. **Integration:** this is a real work session, not a formality — expect to spend real time on it, and expect bugs specifically at the boundaries (a name mismatch in a foreign key, an auth claim you assumed exists but doesn't, a CORS issue between real deployed services). This is normal for team projects, not a sign anything was done wrong.
4. **Post-integration:** yes, you'll likely come back to your page at least once more — most commonly to fix a boundary assumption that turned out wrong once real data from a teammate's table showed up, or to adjust after a schema tweak the team agreed on collectively.

The realistic goal isn't "never touch it again" — it's "the only things I touch later are the seams I already know about," which is exactly the list above. Worth writing that list into your C1/C2 reflection now, actually — "known integration debt, deliberately deferred" is a stronger reflection than pretending the standalone build was integration-complete.

Want me to turn that seam list into a short integration checklist document now, so it's ready to hand to your team (and to yourself) when that phase starts?

text:
The user is asking whether the three mobile screens for the on-ground app—QR Fallback, Log Exception, and Critical Alert—can coexist in the same project folder as the exception admin page. I'm considering the technical architecture here, since the on-ground app is a mobile-web staff view separate from the admin interface, so I need to think through whether they can share the same project structure or if they need to be isolated. So I should confirm with the user whether they're thinking of this as mobile-web views within the same React+Vite app, or if they actually need a separate native/PWA codebase for on-ground staff. Given the context that the QR check-in was already scoped as a mobile-web view in the same project, it's reasonable to assume these new screens follow the same pattern—but I should ask for confirmation before proceeding with the build, since this assumption shapes the entire architecture.Yes — and I'd actually recommend it. Here's the reasoning, plus one assumption I want to confirm before we start building.

## Why they can share a project

Your on-ground screens (QR Fallback, Log Exception, Critical Alert — Screens 9–11) aren't a different technology from your admin inbox. They're still React components rendered by the same Vite app; the only real difference is they're designed mobile-first because on-ground staff will be using them on a phone. "Separate interface" describes the *user experience* (staff-in-the-field vs. admin-at-a-desk), not a separate codebase. Your own project already treats it this way — recall `QRCheckInPage.jsx` was scaffolded as just another route (`/checkin`) inside the same `App.jsx`, tagged as "mobile-web staff view." Your three screens are the same pattern.

Practically, sharing the project means:

- One `npm install`, one `vite.config.js`, one build
- You reuse `tokens.css`, `StatusBadge.jsx`, and your existing `exceptionsApi.js` data layer instead of duplicating them
- Your backend (`server/`) already has almost everything these screens need — QR fallback and critical alert are really just different entry points into the same `exceptions` table and alert fan-out you already built

## How I'd structure it in the folder

Same standalone project, new routes alongside `/exceptions`:

```
src/pages/
  ExceptionInboxPage.jsx        (existing — admin/desktop view)
  onground/
    QRFallbackPage.jsx          ★ new
    LogExceptionOnGroundPage.jsx ★ new
    CriticalAlertPage.jsx       ★ new
```

`App.jsx` gets a couple more routes (e.g. `/onground/qr-fallback`, `/onground/log`, `/onground/alert`), all still with no login gate, same as your current standalone build. Since these are meant to be used on a phone, I'd default their layout to mobile viewport styling first (unlike the admin inbox, which is desktop-first with a mobile fallback).

## One thing to confirm before I build

I'm assuming these three screens are **still web pages** — same React/Vite stack, just viewed at phone width, matching how your team already treated `QRCheckInPage`. If instead your team intends the on-ground experience to eventually be a real native app or PWA (separate framework, installable, camera API access for QR scanning, etc.), that's a different build — still could live in the same repo, but as a genuinely separate app, not just new routes.

Is it the "same web app, phone-width routes" approach, or do you know it needs to be a real native/installable app for camera access?

text:
I'm thinking through the architecture here—the user needs two separate frontend applications that share a backend, and possibly a shared design-tokens package to keep things consistent. The admin app already exists, so I need to plan how the new on-ground app fits into this structure and confirm the approach before scaffolding it out. The key trade-off is that keeping them as truly separate applications means no shared imports across the boundary — they'd each have their own package.json, routing, and entry point, though they can duplicate design tokens and components like StatusBadge. Before I restructure his existing project by moving the current frontend into an admin-app subfolder and creating onground-app as a sibling, I should confirm this reorganization plan with him since it's a significant structural change to what he already has.Good clarification — that changes the structure meaningfully, and it's worth getting right before I start moving files around, since it means restructuring what you already have.

## Why "two connected apps" is a different shape than "two more routes"

If they were the same app, the on-ground screens would just be new routes inside your current `App.jsx`. But you're describing two genuinely separate products — different users, different devices, likely different deployment URLs later (e.g. `admin.mustergo.app` vs `field.mustergo.app`), and eventually possibly different tech (web vs installable). That means:

- **Two separate frontend projects** — each with its own `package.json`, `vite.config.js`, `App.jsx`, entry point, and `npm install`/`npm run dev`. Not two folders sharing one build.
- **No shared imports across the boundary.** The admin app and the on-ground app shouldn't `import` each other's components. If they need the same thing (design tokens, `StatusBadge`), each app gets its own copy — because "connected but separate applications" specifically means neither breaks if the other changes.
- **One shared backend.** This is the "connected" part — both apps talk to the same `server/` (same MySQL/Supabase database, same `exceptions` table), just from different UIs suited to different users. That's exactly how a real admin-dashboard-plus-field-app product works.

## Proposed folder structure

```
mustergo-project/                 ← everything for your review lives here
├── admin-app/                    (your existing standalone build, moved in)
│   ├── src/  (ExceptionInboxPage, LogExceptionModal, exceptionsApi.js...)
│   └── package.json
├── onground-app/                 ★ new, separate project
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── pages/
│   │   │   ├── QRFallbackPage.jsx
│   │   │   ├── LogExceptionPage.jsx
│   │   │   └── CriticalAlertPage.jsx
│   │   └── lib/exceptionsApi.js   (own copy — same shape, own simulation data)
│   └── package.json
└── server/                       (shared — unchanged, both apps point at it)
```

Each app runs independently (`cd admin-app && npm run dev` on one port, `cd onground-app && npm run dev` on another), and each is fully demoable in `USE_SIMULATION` mode on its own — which fits your review goal for both, without either depending on the other being open.

Good clarification — that changes the structure meaningfully, and it's worth getting right before I start moving files around, since it means restructuring what you already have.

## Why "two connected apps" is a different shape than "two more routes"

If they were the same app, the on-ground screens would just be new routes inside your current `App.jsx`. But you're describing two genuinely separate products — different users, different devices, likely different deployment URLs later (e.g. `admin.mustergo.app` vs `field.mustergo.app`), and eventually possibly different tech (web vs installable). That means:

- **Two separate frontend projects** — each with its own `package.json`, `vite.config.js`, `App.jsx`, entry point, and `npm install`/`npm run dev`. Not two folders sharing one build.
- **No shared imports across the boundary.** The admin app and the on-ground app shouldn't `import` each other's components. If they need the same thing (design tokens, `StatusBadge`), each app gets its own copy — because "connected but separate applications" specifically means neither breaks if the other changes.
- **One shared backend.** This is the "connected" part — both apps talk to the same `server/` (same MySQL/Supabase database, same `exceptions` table), just from different UIs suited to different users. That's exactly how a real admin-dashboard-plus-field-app product works.

## Proposed folder structure

```
mustergo-project/                 ← everything for your review lives here
├── admin-app/                    (your existing standalone build, moved in)
│   ├── src/  (ExceptionInboxPage, LogExceptionModal, exceptionsApi.js...)
│   └── package.json
├── onground-app/                 ★ new, separate project
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── pages/
│   │   │   ├── QRFallbackPage.jsx
│   │   │   ├── LogExceptionPage.jsx
│   │   │   └── CriticalAlertPage.jsx
│   │   └── lib/exceptionsApi.js   (own copy — same shape, own simulation data)
│   └── package.json
└── server/                       (shared — unchanged, both apps point at it)
```

Each app runs independently (`cd admin-app && npm run dev` on one port, `cd onground-app && npm run dev` on another), and each is fully demoable in `USE_SIMULATION` mode on its own — which fits your review goal for both, without either depending on the other being open.

On the substance, two separate decisions to react to:

## Neon over Supabase — reasonable, and here's why

My Supabase recommendation was specifically weighted on its built-in auth service saving your team from hand-rolling one. If your teammate has already built a custom auth file, that specific advantage disappears — so Neon becomes an equally good (arguably simpler) choice. Both are serverless Postgres; the actual database experience is nearly identical, and your schema/query rewrite work (MySQL → Postgres syntax) is the same either way regardless of which one you'd picked. Neon's free tier is also fine for a student project. No objection here — it's a legitimate call, not a downgrade.

## The custom auth file — this is the part that actually needs specifics

This is the piece that determines how much of my `requireAuth` stub needs to change later, so before integration happens, you'll want to get these details from him (not urgent now, but worth capturing):

- **What does his login endpoint return?** A JWT? A session cookie? A Supabase-style access token? This determines how your Express middleware verifies it.
- **What's in the token/session** — does it carry a `role` claim (staff vs admin), a user ID you can foreign-key against, anything your `raised_by`/`resolved_by` columns need?
- **What's his users table called and shaped?** Your `exceptions.raised_by` and `resolved_by` currently point at a `users` table you stubbed — his real one needs to match in ID type/format (likely `uuid` in Postgres) for your foreign keys to work.
- **Does he expose a shared verification approach** (e.g. a secret or public key you can independently verify tokens with), or does every protected route need to call his auth service to check validity? That affects whether your `exceptions` routes stay fast and self-contained or gain a network dependency.

None of this blocks what we're doing right now — you're heads-down on the on-ground app for your review, and integration is deliberately still ahead of us, exactly per the mindset we agreed on last message. I'd just flag it to your teammate as a short "what does your auth file return and what's the users table shaped like" question whenever you two next sync, so it's answered before integration day rather than discovered during it.

-- ============================================================================
-- MusterGo — Exception Logging + QR attendance (Owner: Jayden)
-- Database: PostgreSQL (Neon)
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Owned tables: exceptions, exception_alerts, attendance.
-- The users/trips/coaches/delegates tables are shared/teammate territory —
-- included here as minimal stubs so this module runs standalone. In the
-- integrated Neon project, drop the stubs and keep only the owned tables.
-- Enum-like columns use TEXT + CHECK (portable, easy to migrate).
-- ============================================================================

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS attendance CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS exception_alerts CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS exceptions CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS delegates CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS coaches CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS trips CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users CASCADE;

-- ---- Shared / teammate stubs ------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name          TEXT NOT NULL,
  email         TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  role          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'staff' CHECK (role IN ('admin','staff')),
  password_hash TEXT,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE trips (
  id         TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  start_date DATE,
  end_date   DATE,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE coaches (
  id       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_id  TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES trips(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  label    TEXT NOT NULL,
  capacity INT  NOT NULL DEFAULT 40
);

CREATE TABLE delegates (
  id       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_id  TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES trips(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  name     TEXT NOT NULL,
  coach_id TEXT REFERENCES coaches(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  is_vip   BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);

-- ---- Owned: exceptions (Support Tickets CRUD) -------------------------------
CREATE TABLE exceptions (
  id              TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_id         TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES trips(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  delegate_id     TEXT REFERENCES delegates(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  coach_id        TEXT REFERENCES coaches(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  issue_type      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (issue_type IN
                    ('MISSING_PERSON','LOST_BADGE','FACE_MATCH_FAILED','DEAD_PHONE','VIP_REQUEST','OTHER')),
  priority        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NORMAL' CHECK (priority IN ('CRITICAL','NORMAL','LOW')),
  status          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN' CHECK (status IN ('OPEN','RESOLVED','CANCELLED')),
  is_critical     BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  note            TEXT,
  raised_by       TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  resolved_by     TEXT REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  resolution_note TEXT,
  client_ref      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,           -- offline idempotency key
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  resolved_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
  deleted_at      TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_exc_trip_status   ON exceptions (trip_id, status);
CREATE INDEX idx_exc_trip_priority ON exceptions (trip_id, priority);
CREATE INDEX idx_exc_delegate      ON exceptions (delegate_id);

-- ---- Owned: exception_alerts (real-time fan-out, one row per recipient) ------
CREATE TABLE exception_alerts (
  id              TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  exception_id    TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES exceptions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  recipient_id    TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  ack_status      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING' CHECK (ack_status IN ('PENDING','ACKNOWLEDGED','ON_IT')),
  delivered_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  acknowledged_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (exception_id, recipient_id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_alert_recipient ON exception_alerts (recipient_id, ack_status);

-- ---- Owned: attendance (QR / manual head-count) -----------------------------
CREATE TABLE attendance (
  id           TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  trip_id      TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES trips(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  delegate_id  TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES delegates(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  method       TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'QR' CHECK (method IN ('QR','FACE','MANUAL')),
  status       TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PRESENT' CHECK (status IN ('PRESENT','ABSENT')),
  marked_by    TEXT REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (trip_id, delegate_id)                    -- one attendance row per delegate per trip
);
CREATE INDEX idx_att_trip ON attendance (trip_id, status);
EOF

content.thinking:
Postgres 16 is installed with a cluster at /var/lib/postgresql/16/main on port 5432, but it's currently stopped. I need to start it and run the full test sequence in one bash call to avoid losing the daemon between commands—starting postgres, creating the database and user, loading the schema and seed data, running the Node app, and testing with curl. Since Postgres must run as the `postgres` user rather than root, I'll use the Debian wrapper `pg_ctlcluster` to start the cluster.

I'll need to ensure /var/run/postgresql exists and is owned by postgres, then start the cluster and wait for it to be ready. For the app to connect over TCP to 127.0.0.1:5432, I need to create a role with a password (the default `postgres` user uses peer authentication on the socket). I'll create a role `mgapp` with a password, set the app's DATABASE_URL to `postgresql://mgapp:[REDACTED]@127.0.0.1:5432/mustergo` with SSL disabled, and load the schema and seed data as that user. The default pg_hba.conf should already allow password-based connections from localhost.

I'm setting up the role and database creation commands to run as the postgres user, then loading the schema and seed files using the mgapp credentials over TCP, and finally starting the node server with the appropriate environment variables.

cat > /tmp/pgtest.sh << 'SCRIPT'
set -e
SRV=/home/claude/mustergo-project/server
mkdir -p /var/run/postgresql && chown postgres:postgres /var/run/postgresql
pg_ctlcluster 16 main start >/tmp/pgstart.log 2>&1 || true
for i in $(seq 1 30); do pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432 >/dev/null 2>&1 && break; sleep 1; done
echo "postgres: $(pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432 2>&1 | tail -1)"

# role + db (idempotent)
su postgres -c "psql -tewbc \"DO \\$\\$ BEGIN IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='mgapp') THEN CREATE ROLE mgapp LOGIN PASSWORD 'mgpass'; END IF; END \\$\\$;\"" >/tmp/role.log 2>&1 || true
su postgres -c "psql -tc \"SELECT 1 FROM pg_database WHERE datname='mustergo'\" | grep -q 1 || psql -c 'CREATE DATABASE mustergo OWNER mgapp;'" >/tmp/db.log 2>&1 || true
echo "role+db ready"

export PGPASSWORD=mgpass
psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U mgapp -d mustergo -q -f "$SRV/db/schema.sql" && echo "schema loaded"
psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U mgapp -d mustergo -q -f "$SRV/db/seed.sql" && echo "seed loaded"
echo "row check:"; psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U mgapp -d mustergo -tAc "SELECT priority||'/'||status||'='||count(*) FROM exceptions GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1;" | tr '\n' ' '; echo

cd "$SRV"
[ -d node_modules ] || npm install --no-audit --no-fund >/tmp/srvnpm.log 2>&1
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://mgapp:[REDACTED]@127.0.0.1:5432/mustergo" PGSSL=disable JWT_SECRET=demo
node src/index.js >/tmp/api.log 2>&1 &
APID=$!; sleep 3
echo "=== health ==="; curl -s localhost:4000/api/health; echo
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:4000/api/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"admin@sccci.org"}' | python3 -c "import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['token'])")
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
echo "=== list summary ==="; curl -s "localhost:4000/api/exceptions?tripId=trip-bj" -H "$AUTH" | python3 -c "import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['summary'])"
echo "=== QR scan check-in (Screen 1) ==="; curl -s -X POST localhost:4000/api/attendance/scan -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"tripId":"trip-bj","delegateId":"d-lim","method":"QR"}' | python3 -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print(d['status'],'->',d['delegate']['name'],d['delegate']['coach'],'VIP' if d['delegate']['vip'] else '')"
echo "=== QR scan unknown badge (defective path) ==="; curl -s -o /dev/null -w "unknown badge -> HTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST localhost:4000/api/attendance/scan -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"tripId":"trip-bj","delegateId":"d-nope","method":"QR"}'
echo "=== headcount ==="; curl -s "localhost:4000/api/attendance/trip-bj" -H "$AUTH"; echo
echo "=== create critical (Screen 2 -> appears on admin) ==="; NEW=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:4000/api/exceptions -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"tripId":"trip-bj","delegateId":"d-goh","issueType":"MISSING_PERSON","note":"onground test","markCritical":true}')
echo "$NEW" | python3 -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print('created',d['priority'],d['status'],'alert='+str(d['alertDispatched']),'recipients='+str(d['recipients']))"
NID=$(echo "$NEW" | python3 -c "import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['id'])")
echo "=== ack the alert (Screen 3 'I'm on it') ==="; curl -s -X PATCH "localhost:4000/api/exceptions/$NID/ack" -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"status":"ON_IT"}' | python3 -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print('ack ->',d['status'],'| breakdown',d['breakdown'])"
echo "=== resolve + concurrency guard ==="; curl -s -X PATCH "localhost:4000/api/exceptions/$NID/resolve" -H "$AUTH" -d '{}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' | python3 -c "import sys,json;print('resolve ->',json.load(sys.stdin)['status'])"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "resolve again -> HTTP %{http_code}\n" -X PATCH "localhost:4000/api/exceptions/$NID/resolve" -H "$AUTH" -d '{}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
kill $APID 2>/dev/null || true
pg_ctlcluster 16 main stop >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
SCRIPT

input.description: Step-by-step Neon Postgres activation guide
input.file_text:
# Activating Neon Postgres

The backend now runs on **PostgreSQL (Neon)** instead of MySQL. Here's how to point it at a live Neon database and turn the whole thing on.

## 1. Get a connection string
Your teammate owns the Neon project (`wispy-flower-...`). Two options:
- **Shared (recommended):** ask him to add you to the Neon project, or to send you the connection string for a `mustergo` database. Neon dashboard → your project → **Connection Details** → copy the **Connection string** (it looks like `postgresql://user:pass@ep-xxxx.ap-southeast-1.aws.neon.tech/mustergo?sslmode=require`).
- **Your own (for solo testing):** create a free project at neon.tech, add a database called `mustergo`, and copy its connection string.

> Because his auth and your tables will eventually share one database, coordinate early on whether your `exceptions`/`attendance` tables live in the same database (they can) and whether your foreign keys point at his real `users`/`delegates` tables or your stubs (stubs for now, his tables at integration).

## 2. Configure the server
```bash
cd server
cp .env.example .env
```
Open `.env` and paste your string into `DATABASE_URL`. Leave the `DB_*` fallback vars as-is (they're only used if `DATABASE_URL` is empty).

## 3. Load the schema + seed into Neon
Either use `psql` locally:
```bash
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f db/schema.sql
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f db/seed.sql
```
…or open the **Neon SQL Editor** in the dashboard, paste the contents of `db/schema.sql`, run it, then do the same with `db/seed.sql`.

## 4. Start the API
```bash
npm install        # installs pg
npm start
```
Visit `http://localhost:4000/api/health` — you should see `{"ok":true,"db":"postgres"}`. If it says `unreachable`, the connection string or SSL is wrong (Neon needs `?sslmode=require`, which the pool handles automatically).

## 5. Connect the two frontends
In **both** `admin-app/src/lib/exceptionsApi.js` and `onground-app/src/lib/exceptionsApi.js`:
- set `USE_SIMULATION = false`

Then create a `.env` in each app folder:
```
VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000/api
```
Restart each app (`npm run dev`). Now a log raised on the on-ground app appears on the admin inbox, and critical alerts fan out to every connected device over SSE — all backed by Neon.

## Local Postgres instead of Neon (optional)
If you'd rather test without Neon, install Postgres locally, leave `DATABASE_URL` empty, set the `DB_*` vars, and uncomment `PGSSL=disable`. Everything else is identical.

## What changed from the MySQL version
- `mysql2` → `pg`; `db/pool.js` now builds a Postgres pool from `DATABASE_URL`.
- Schema is Postgres dialect: `TEXT`+`CHECK` instead of `ENUM`, `BOOLEAN` instead of `TINYINT`, `TIMESTAMPTZ`, and `COUNT(*) FILTER (...)` for the summary counts.
- All queries use `$1, $2` placeholders and `RETURNING`/`rowCount`.
- New endpoints for the on-ground app: `POST /api/attendance/scan` (QR check-in), `PATCH /api/exceptions/:id/ack` (alert acknowledge), plus manual override and head-count.

input.description: Top-level project README covering both apps, the shared backend, and how to run everything
input.file_text:
# MusterGo — Jayden's feature (two connected apps + shared backend)

Two separate front-end applications that share one Neon Postgres backend:

```
mustergo-project/
├── admin-app/       Office admin web app — Exception Inbox (desktop-first, responsive)
├── onground-app/    Staff phone app — QR check-in, Log exception, Critical alerts (mobile-first)
├── server/          Shared API — Node/Express + Neon Postgres (both apps talk to this)
├── badges/          Scannable QR test badges (badge-sheet.html + PNGs)
├── docs/            A1 documents (use cases, API doc, DB schema)
└── NEON_SETUP.md    How to switch the DB on
```

The two apps never import each other — the only thing connecting them is the shared API. That's deliberate: either can change without breaking the other.

## Quick demo (no backend, no database)
Each app is self-contained in **simulation mode** (`USE_SIMULATION = true`), which is how you demo them for the progress review.

```bash
# Admin app  → http://localhost:5173
cd admin-app && npm install && npm run dev

# On-ground app → http://localhost:5174   (separate terminal)
cd onground-app && npm install && npm run dev
```

- **Admin app:** opens straight into the Exception Inbox (filter, log, resolve, cancel).
- **On-ground app:** opens on the home screen with a live critical alert. **Scan** tab = camera QR check-in, **Issues → Log** = raise an exception. Logging a critical one makes the alert appear on the home screen.

## The three on-ground screens
1. **Scan (QR check-in)** — real camera via `getUserMedia` + `jsQR`. A valid badge marks attendance; a damaged/unknown badge shows the "not recognised" prompt and offers Log exception. Test badges are in `badges/` (open `badge-sheet.html` and scan it).
2. **Log exception** — same idea as the admin form, phone-sized. Creating a log sends it to the backend where it appears on the admin inbox.
3. **Critical alert (home)** — incoming critical alerts land here with Acknowledge / I'm on it, backed by the `PATCH /api/exceptions/:id/ack` endpoint.

## Camera notes
`getUserMedia` needs a **secure context**. It works on `localhost` automatically. To test on a real phone over your Wi-Fi, run `npm run dev:https` in `onground-app` (serves over TLS; accept the self-signed cert warning) — otherwise the browser blocks the camera off localhost.

## Connected mode (log on phone → shows on admin)
This needs the shared backend running on Neon — see **NEON_SETUP.md**. In short: start `server/`, set `USE_SIMULATION = false` in both apps, add `VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000/api` to each app's `.env`, and restart. Then logs and alerts flow between the two apps in real time.

## Verified locally
- Both apps build cleanly (`vite build`).
- Backend runs against real PostgreSQL: health, login, list/summary, QR check-in (+ 404 on unknown badge), head-count, create-critical (5-device fan-out), acknowledge, resolve, and the 409 concurrency guard all pass.
- QR pipeline: generated badges decode with the same `jsQR` the camera uses and validate as check-ins; a malformed code is correctly rejected.

set -e
P=/home/claude/mustergo-project
O=/mnt/user-data/outputs/mustergo-project
rm -rf "$O"; mkdir -p "$O/screenshots" "$O/badges"

# on-ground screenshots
cp "$P/onground-app/shots/1-home-alert.png"     "$O/screenshots/onground-1-home-alert.png"
cp "$P/onground-app/shots/6-scan-live.png"      "$O/screenshots/onground-2-scan-live.png"
cp "$P/onground-app/shots/4-scan-checkedin.png" "$O/screenshots/onground-3-scan-checkedin.png"
cp "$P/onground-app/shots/3-scan-defective.png" "$O/screenshots/onground-4-scan-defective.png"
cp "$P/onground-app/shots/2-log-exception.png"  "$O/screenshots/onground-5-log-exception.png"
cp "$P/onground-app/shots/5-log-to-alert.png"   "$O/screenshots/onground-6-log-to-alert.png"

# guides at top level of the output
cp "$P/README.md" "$P/NEON_SETUP.md" "$O/"

find . -name node_modules -type d -prune -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null || true

echo; echo "zip size:"; du -h "$O/mustergo-project.zip" | cut -f1

Done — the on-ground app is built, both apps and the Neon-Postgres backend are verified, and everything's packaged in `mustergo-project.zip`.

**The three screens (all functioning, matched to your Figma)**

1. **Scan** — a real camera scanner using `getUserMedia` + `jsQR`. Point it at a badge: a valid one marks attendance and shows the green "checked in" banner; a damaged or unknown code shows the red "not recognised" prompt and offers Log exception as the fallback. I couldn't point a physical camera at the sandbox, so I proved the decode pipeline instead: generated badges decode with the *same* jsQR the camera runs and validate as check-ins (5/5), and a malformed code is correctly rejected. The `badge-sheet.html` in `badges/` has scannable QR codes — open it and scan it to test for real.
2. **Log exception** — the phone version of your admin form. Submitting a critical log fans it out and lands you on the home screen with the alert (screenshot 6 shows that flow).
3. **Critical alert (home)** — incoming alerts with Acknowledge / I'm on it, wired to the new `PATCH /api/exceptions/:id/ack` endpoint.

**Database switched to Neon Postgres.** The backend now uses `pg` with a `DATABASE_URL` connection string. I installed a real Postgres locally and ran the full suite against it — health, QR check-in (+ 404 on unknown badge), head-count, create-critical (5-device fan-out), acknowledge, resolve, and the 409 concurrency guard all pass. **NEON_SETUP.md** has the exact activation steps: get the connection string, paste it into `server/.env`, load `schema.sql` + `seed.sql`, `npm start`, then flip `USE_SIMULATION = false` in both apps.

**Structure** — your two apps are now siblings sharing one backend: `admin-app/`, `onground-app/`, and `server/`. They don't import each other; the only link is the shared API, which is exactly what makes "log on the phone → appears on admin" work once you're in connected mode.

**Two honest notes for your review:**
- Each app demos standalone in simulation mode (no backend needed) — that's your safest review setup. The cross-app "phone log shows on admin" behaviour specifically requires the shared server running on Neon, per NEON_SETUP.md.
- For camera testing on an actual phone (not your laptop), you need `npm run dev:https` because browsers block the camera on non-localhost HTTP. On your laptop's localhost it just works.

Want me to wire up the connected mode next (both apps pointed at the running server so you can demo a phone log appearing live on the admin inbox), or leave that for after the review?

I've now read every file. Their frontend builds cleanly. Here's the full picture.

## What their repo has that we're missing

**A real, working shared backend.** `backend/server.js` + `data.js` on Express + `pg` (Postgres) — already Neon-compatible, auto-detecting SSL from `DATABASE_URL`. It auto-creates its schema and seeds a trip, 4 coaches, and a login on first run. Nobody sets up tables by hand.

**A permission system, not just roles.** `permissions.js` at the repo root is imported by *both* frontend and backend: `manageDelegates`, `exportData`, `manageAccounts`. Routes are gated with `requirePermission("...")`, and there's an `AccountControlPage` for managing accounts. This is more sophisticated than the plain `staff`/`admin` role I stubbed.

**Real auth with live session revocation.** `POST /api/auth/login` takes `{ staffId, password }` (not email), returns a base64 demo token plus a permissions object. `GET /api/auth/session` re-reads permissions from the DB so someone can be logged out mid-session. Login is `staff_194` / `password123!`.

**Two governing documents I hadn't seen.** `HIGH_LEVEL_DESIGN.md` contains the authoritative DDL and REST API table — **including your endpoints**. `PROJECT_IMPLEMENTATION_PHASE.md` assigns you: exception CRUD + inbox, the Log Exception mobile flow, manual override, and the QR-fallback path shared with Vimal.

**An explicit ownership convention.** Every base file carries a "DO NOT edit this file" banner from Jun Qi, and `server.js` has a marked **TEAMMATE ZONE** where you mount your own router:
```js
import exceptionsRouter from "./routes/exceptions.js";
app.use(exceptionsRouter);
```

**Also: `AccountControlPage`, an Excel export endpoint, a `/api` dev proxy, and `apiDelete`** — which their `api.js` has and my old copy didn't.

## Where my build conflicts with theirs

This is the important part, and it's not a small list.

| Thing | Mine | Theirs (authoritative) |
|---|---|---|
| Exception table | `exceptions` | **`exception_tickets`** |
| Issue column | `issue_type` | **`type`** |
| Idempotency key | `client_ref` | **`client_event_id`** |
| Endpoints | `/api/exceptions` | **`/api/trips/:id/exceptions`** |
| Login body | `{ email }` | **`{ staffId, password }`** |
| Auth model | my own JWT + `staff`/`admin` | **their token + permissions object** |
| Attendance table | `attendance` | **`check_in_logs`** |
| Delegate IDs | `d-lim`, `trip-bj` | **`d-1`…, trip `t-1`, coaches `c1`–`c4`** |
| Statuses | OPEN/RESOLVED/CANCELLED | **OPEN/RESOLVED only** |

Two more things worth flagging:

**Their live backend doesn't create your tables.** `data.js` only creates `trips`, `coaches`, `delegates`, `accounts` — no `exception_tickets`, no `check_in_logs`. The HLD specifies them, but nobody's implemented them. That's *your* job, and since you can't edit `data.js`, your router needs to create its own tables on startup.

**A real bug you should raise with the team:** `frontend/src/lib/api.js` imports `../../../permissions.js` — a file *outside* the `frontend/` folder. Vite's dev server handles it via `fs.allow: ['..']`, and `vite build` worked here. But when Vercel deploys with `frontend/` as the root directory, that parent file won't exist in the build context and the deploy will fail. Worth flagging now, not on deployment day.

## How to integrate — the approach that respects their rules

**Backend:** create `backend/routes/exceptions.js` (a new file — you own it), exporting a Router that (a) creates `exception_tickets` + `check_in_logs` with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, and (b) implements the HLD's endpoints. Mount it with two lines in the TEAMMATE ZONE. Nothing of Jun Qi's is touched.

**Admin frontend:** drop in `pages/ExceptionInboxPage.jsx` (replacing their scaffold — it's tagged *Owner · Jayden*), plus your CSS and modal, and rewrite your data layer to use *their* `api.js` (`apiGet`/`apiPost`/`apiPatch`/`apiDelete`) so you inherit their token handling for free. Their `App.jsx` and `Sidebar.jsx` already route `/exceptions` to you — no edits needed to either.

**On-ground app:** stays a separate app. It just points at the same backend and calls the same endpoints.

The real work is a **contract adaptation**: renaming tables/columns/endpoints to match the HLD, and swapping my auth stub for their token. Your UI, CSS, business rules, QR scanner, and alert logic all survive unchanged.

One thing genuinely undecided that you should ask the team about: **the HLD says nothing about real-time push.** My critical-alert feature uses SSE, and their backend has no WebSocket/SSE layer. Your "push to all staff devices" requirement needs *some* transport — SSE is the simplest thing that fits their Express app, but it means adding something the HLD didn't plan for, and Vimal/Vance may have assumptions here.

Real-time headcount & attendance reconciliation for SCCCI overseas delegations.
